newsitem.title: USA: Protest prompts Republicans to review TV advertisement.
newsitem.headline: Protest prompts Republicans to review TV advertisement.

text.p: The California Republican Party said on Wednesday it was reviewing a planned commercial against affirmative action featuring a famous speech by Dr. Martin Luther King after his estate protested.

News that the party planned to use an excerpt from King's "I have a dream" speech in a television ad supporting Proposition 209, which would ban state affirmative action programmes based on race or sex, caused a furore.

Several civil rights leaders condemned the use of King's words in the ad, and the company that manages the King estate asked the makers of the commercial not to use the slain civil rights leader's words or image.

Phillip Jones, president of Atlanta-based Intellectual Properties Management Inc., said the company did not allow King's copyrighted speeches to be used in partisan commercials. "We don't feel it's appropriate. We've always had this policy," Jones said.
About 100 protesters held a demonstration against the planned commercial at the Martin Luther King Jr. Fountain in San Francisco on Wednesday.

Also on Wednesday, police in Los Angeles dressed in riot gear and some on horseback arrested 34 protesters who blocked a major roadway outside a federal building during a demonstration against Proposition 209.

A police spokesman said the demonstrators were arrested for failing to disperse and blocking Wilshire Boulevard in Westwood near the campus of UCLA. He said the District Attorney's office would determine whether to press charges against the 34 who were arrested in the peaceful protest.

Californians are due to vote Nov. 5 on the controversial Proposition 209, which would roll back affirmative action programmes used since the 1960s to increase opportunities for women and racial minorities.

The Republican-funded commercial originally due for release in California on Wednesday featured an excerpt from King's 1963 speech in which he said he dreamed of a society where people "will not be judged by the colour of their skin but the content of their character."

California Republican Party spokeswoman Victoria Herrington said on Wednesday the party would "relook" at the ad and would be sensitive to the King estate's concerns, but said no decision had yet been taken on whether to drop the King excerpt.
The start of the ad campaign would be delayed for a few days, she said. "The California Republican Party intends to do a very strong pro-Proposition 209 ad campaign," she added.

King copyrighted all of his speeches during his lifetime, Jones said. The commercial's use of King's words to suggest he would not have supported affirmative action was inaccurate, because King had stated in his writings that he was in favour of affirmative action, he said.
